questions.q: Which table should a real SLA report be built against?
options: `task_sla`, since it holds one row per SLA instance with breach and percentage data
`incident`, since it already carries a priority field
`cmn_schedule`, since it defines business hours
`contract_sla`, since it defines the SLA targets
questions.explain: `task_sla` is the running-instance table with `has_breached` and `business_percentage` — `incident` doesn't carry that detail directly.

questions.q: Why might an incident have more than one `task_sla` record over its life?
options: It never can — exactly one `task_sla` row exists per incident
Every incident automatically gets one `task_sla` row per day it stays open
More than one SLA Definition can apply at once, such as a separate Response SLA and Resolution SLA
`task_sla` rows are created only after an incident is closed
questions.explain: If multiple SLA Definitions' Applies To conditions match the same record, each creates its own task_sla instance.

questions.q: What does grouping breached `task_sla` records by Assignment Group help you determine, as distinct from grouping by Priority?
options: Whether a specific team's performance is driving breaches, versus whether the target itself is unrealistic
Nothing — the two groupings always produce the same answer
Whether the SLA Definition's Start condition is configured correctly
The exact business schedule attached to the SLA Definition
questions.explain: By Assignment Group surfaces a team-performance signal; by Priority surfaces whether the target is realistic. Running both distinguishes the two.

questions.q: Why is average `business_percentage` consumed a more honest signal than breach count alone?
options: It isn't — breach count is always sufficient on its own
It replaces the need for a Stop condition
Two teams can share an identical low breach rate while one runs much closer to breaching than the other, and percentage consumed reveals that margin
`business_percentage` only applies to Priority 1 incidents
questions.explain: A 0% breach rate can hide a team running at 99% of target versus one at 40% — breach count alone can't tell them apart.

questions.q: When is Performance Analytics the better tool than a standard Report for SLA data?
options: Performance Analytics cannot be used with `task_sla` data
When you want to change the SLA Definition's Pause condition
When you only need a single point-in-time snapshot of today's breach rate
When the real question is whether breach rate is improving or worsening over time, as a trend
questions.explain: Performance Analytics builds a real time series with trend lines, which a point-in-time Report or pivot table cannot show.
